insider_note: The exponent 5/2 never actually has to be handled as a fraction — it cancels completely the moment the two forms are added, because sin^(5/2)x + cos^(5/2)x appears in both the numerator sum and the denominator.

steps.label: Apply the property with a = π/2
steps.margin_note: One mark. Label the given integral (1) before transforming it.
steps.memory_tip: Any power of cosx or sinx follows the same swap rule under x → π/2 − x — only the base changes, not the exponent.
steps.why: Labelling the original integral (1) sets up the transformed second form that the addition step needs.
common_mistakes: Not writing the property statement before using it.
Confusing which integral is (1) in the working.

steps.label: Write the second form
steps.margin_note: One more mark. cos^(5/2)x becomes sin^(5/2)x under the swap, and the denominator's two terms swap places but stay the same sum.
steps.memory_tip: cos^(5/2)(π/2 − x) = sin^(5/2)x — the base swaps, the power 5/2 stays exactly as written.
steps.why: Under the swap x → π/2 − x, cosx becomes sinx everywhere the base appears, while the denominator (a sum of both powers) reappears unchanged since it already contains both terms.
common_mistakes: Writing the new numerator as cos^(5/2)x instead of sin^(5/2)x.
Changing the order of the denominator's two terms and thinking that changes its value.

steps.label: Add and solve
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. The numerator sum equals the denominator exactly, so the fraction becomes 1.
steps.memory_tip: Whenever numerator1 + numerator2 = denominator exactly, the integral of the sum is just ∫1 dx.
steps.why: The sum in the numerator is identical to the denominator, so the whole fraction equals 1 for every x — reducing the integral to the length of the interval.
common_mistakes: Not recognising that the added numerator exactly matches the denominator.
Forgetting to divide by 2 to isolate I.
